title: Welcome to the packet factory
subtitle: No networking knowledge needed. Start with one small idea.

steps.title: A packet is a little delivery.
steps.body: Imagine sending a message as a collection of small deliveries. This game draws each packet as a crate. The belts stand for its journey through one network device — one hop.
steps.takeaway: You are arranging how one device handles its traffic.
steps.source: RFC 2475 §2.3.1; factory representation is a game metaphor

steps.title: Different deliveries need different care.
steps.body: A live conversation needs steady, timely delivery. A file transfer can share the remaining room. When a connection is busy, queues hold packets and a scheduler decides which queue goes next.
steps.takeaway: Quality of service means choosing how traffic shares a busy connection.

steps.title: The lid tells the sorter what to read.
steps.body: The first six lights form a number called DSCP. A sorter can use that number to choose a lane. The last two, smaller lights are ECN: separate congestion information. They do not change the DSCP number.
steps.takeaway: For your first task, read only the first six lights.

steps.title: Your first job is just one small edit.
steps.body: The first factory is already connected. One sorter rule has a typo: it looks for 47, but the voice crates carry 46. Select the sorter, change its first match value to 46, apply it, and run the trace.
steps.takeaway: You do not need to build a whole factory yet. The guide stays beside the floor.
steps.source: RFC 3246 §2.7; RFC 2475 §2.3.1; task instructions are game rules
